title: Fort Strong
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 13 of 40
content:
Fort Strong brought Cutler back into the room before Danse ever said his name.

Super mutants occupied the island in force. We saw them from the vertibird before landing: huge green figures moving between ruined military buildings, weapons heavy enough to make ordinary people disappear.

Danse became colder with every pass over the target.

Not afraid.

Focused beyond focus.

The pilot banked toward the landing zone.

Danse checked his rifle.

“Primary objective is to clear the fort and secure the ordnance stores.”

I watched him seat the magazine harder than necessary.

“Danse.”

“What?”

“You with me?”

His eyes hardened.

“Of course.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

“This is not the time.”

The aircraft descended.

Fine.

We fought.

Danse did not become reckless. That would have been easier to confront. He remained disciplined, moved with tactical precision, called targets, protected my flank.

But there was anger underneath every shot.

He fired at mutants after they had already gone down. He advanced faster than usual. When one charged, roaring with a sledgehammer raised overhead, Danse met it instead of giving ground.

The impact shook the floor.

“Danse!”

He drove the rifle into the mutant’s throat and fired.

The body fell at his feet.

“Clear,” he said.

Nothing about him was clear.

Inside the fort, the air smelled of old explosives, damp concrete, blood, and the unmistakable musk of super mutant occupation.

We moved room by room.

In a barracks, I found human bones piled in a corner.

Danse stopped beside them.

His breathing changed.

“Keep moving,” he said.

“No.”

His helmet turned.

“We have an objective.”

“We also have thirty seconds.”

“For what?”

“For you to stop pretending this is just another mission.”

His voice went dangerously flat.

“I am not pretending anything.”

“Cutler.”

The name hit like a round against armor.

“Don’t.”

“You told me what happened.”

“That doesn’t make this the time to discuss it.”

“You’re right. The time was before you nearly let that mutant cave your helmet in.”

“I had the situation under control.”

“You had rage under control. That isn’t the same thing.”

Danse stepped closer.

For a moment the power armor made him enormous.

“If my performance is compromising the mission, say so plainly.”

“It is compromising you.”

Silence.

The fluorescent light above us flickered.

I could hear a mutant somewhere deeper in the fort shouting to another.

Danse looked toward the bones.

When he spoke again, his voice was lower.

“Cutler was not the first person I lost to them.”

“I know.”

“He was the one that mattered most.”

“I know.”

His helmet retracted.

Anger had drained from his face, leaving exhaustion.

“I hate them.”

There was no doctrine in the sentence.

Just a man admitting something ugly and true.

“I know.”

“You think that makes me irrational.”

“I think grief can make anyone irrational.”

“That wasn’t the question.”

“No. I think your hatred makes sense.”

He looked surprised.

“I also think it can get you killed.”

There it was.

Both things at once.

Danse leaned one armored shoulder against the wall.

“I don’t know what you expect me to do with that.”

“Nothing right now.”

A long breath.

Then he resealed the helmet.

“Thirty seconds is over.”

“Bossy.”

“Move.”

We finished the mission.

This time Danse fought differently.

Not softer. Not less deadly.

But he stopped chasing targets past cover. He let me take the left corridor without trying to be everywhere at once. When a mutant retreated toward an exposed stairwell, Danse did not follow.

We secured the armory.

On the roof, waiting for extraction, wind tore off the harbor hard enough to sting.

Danse stood at the edge overlooking the water.

I joined him.

“Fort’s secure,” I said.

“Yes.”

“Feel better?”

“No.”

“Good answer.”

He looked over.

“I expected killing them to…”

“Fix something?”

He nodded once.

“It never does.”

“You sound certain.”

“I’ve tried that kind of repair.”

Danse’s gaze returned to the water.

“After Cutler, every super mutant started looking like the one that took him from me.”

I leaned against the railing.

“But the one that took him from you wasn’t a super mutant.”

His expression sharpened.

“You know what I mean.”

“I do.”

The wind filled the silence.

After a minute he said, “The Brotherhood gave me a way to make sense of it.”

“By telling you what the enemy was.”

“Yes.”

“And if the world is more complicated?”

He frowned.

“It doesn’t always get to be.”

That sentence stayed with me.

The vertibird approached from the west.

Danse turned toward it, then stopped.

“Thank you.”

“For yelling at you in a super mutant barracks?”

“For noticing.”

The admission made me still.

He looked uncomfortable immediately.

“I don’t always recognize when I’m allowing personal experience to affect tactical judgment.”

“Everyone needs someone to tell them when they’re being an idiot.”

“That is not what I said.”

“It’s what I heard.”

“Your hearing is defective.”

I grinned.

The vertibird landed.

Danse offered me his hand to help me aboard.

Again, I did not need it.

Again, I took it.

This time his fingers tightened before letting go.

Fort Strong did not give us much room for private thoughts.

Super mutants have a talent for making introspection impractical.

The first one burst from behind a concrete barrier carrying a missile launcher.

Danse shoved me flat behind a burned-out military truck a heartbeat before the rocket crossed the yard.

The explosion punched heat over us.

“Still think I stand too close?” I shouted.

“Yes!”

He rose, fired three controlled shots, and dropped the mutant before it could reload.

A second appeared on the roof.

I caught it with Righteous Authority.

Danse looked at the body, then at me.

“Good shot.”

“Sticker?”

“Focus.”

We fought our way inward.

The fort had been built for soldiers before the bombs and occupied by something else afterward. Old flags hung above walls streaked with blood. Ammunition crates sat beside human bones. In one room somebody had arranged skulls on shelves like trophies.

Danse went very still.

“Savages.”

His voice was colder than I had heard it at ArcJet.

I knew enough now to hear the memory inside the word.

Cutler.

Not the name yet. Only the wound.

We kept moving.

Near the armory a mutant came through a doorway too close for rifles. Danse hit it with the stock of his laser weapon. It grabbed the front of his armor and drove him into the wall hard enough to crack concrete.

I fired into its side.

It turned toward me.

Bad decision for everyone involved.

Danse caught its arm, twisted, and slammed it down. I finished the fight at point-blank range.

For a second there was only our breathing.

Then Danse seized my shoulders.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Did it strike you?”

“No.”

“Were you exposed to—”

“Danse.”

His hands tightened.

The panic in his face was not about me.

Not entirely.

I covered one of his gauntlets with my hand.

“I’m here.”

He stared at me.

The room smelled like scorched meat and dust.

Slowly his grip loosened.

“Yes.”

“I’m not him.”

His expression changed sharply.

I had guessed too close.

“I don’t know who you mean,” I said. “But I’m not him.”

Danse stepped back.

“Continue the sweep.”

The command came rough.

The anger did not leave him when I stopped pushing.

It changed direction.

Danse kicked a spent casing across the floor and immediately looked irritated with himself for the loss of discipline.

“This place killed Dawes,” he said.

I went still.

He had mentioned the name before. Not the details.

“We reconnoitered Fort Strong before the Prydwen arrived. Dawes refused to keep his helmet on. Said it interfered with his peripheral vision.” Danse’s mouth flattened. “A mutant with a super sledge reached him before I could.”

The room around us seemed to tighten.

“You told him to wear it.”

“Repeatedly.”

“And you still blame yourself.”

“I was his commanding officer.”

“There it is again.”

His eyes flashed.

“Command is not decorative.”

“No. But it also doesn’t make you omnipotent.”

He looked away.

That was what Fort Strong had become inside him: Dawes, Cutler, every mutant wearing the outline of someone Danse had failed to save. The hatred made emotional sense even where it made moral reasoning worse.

Understanding it did not mean agreeing with it.

It only told me where the wound was.

I let him have it.

We cleared the rest of the floor in silence.

Only after the last mutant fell did Danse sit on an ammunition crate and remove his helmet.

Sweat ran down his temple.

He looked exhausted in a way the fighting had not caused.

“I owe you an explanation,” he said.

“You don’t owe me your grief.”

His eyes lifted.

“No.”

He looked down at the helmet in his hands.

“But I think I want you to understand it.”

That was different.

I sat on the crate opposite him.

Outside, Brotherhood guns echoed over the fort.

Inside, Danse took a breath that seemed to come from years ago.

“His name was Cutler.”

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
